title: Staged graceful degradation and response sanitization for Dedicated->Hosted routing
creator: Emma Chen
description:
Problem: When tenant traffic is routed from Dedicated capacity to Hosted as a fallback, application-visible regressions can occur: large latency spikes, degraded response formats (missing tool-calls/structured output), and potential leakage of private model variants. Current failover implementations do immediate cutover with minimal transformation, which increases customer confusion and can violate SLAs.

Goal: Implement a staged graceful degradation pipeline that (1) preserves response structure and essential semantics during failover, (2) enforces model variant sanitization and pinned-variant constraints, and (3) progressively relaxes non-essential performance guarantees while keeping latency/SLA bounds observable. This ticket covers design, runtime changes, rollout plan, and QA criteria for the feature.
acceptance_criteria:
A1: Dedicated-first routing remains default; on capacity pressure, requests enter a 3-stage fallback pipeline (prefetch -> trimmed-run -> hosted-backstop) documented below.
A2: Response sanitization layer ensures function/tool-call intents and structured JSON schemas are preserved where possible; failing that, an explicit diagnostic wrapper is returned to callers indicating graceful degradation.
A3: Model variant policy enforcer prevents routing to hosted variants that are not allowed by tenant policy (e.g., private quantized variants).
A4: End-to-end latency degradation curve is documented and monitored: 50th/95th/99th P50/P95/P99 metrics show expected stepwise increase under simulated load tests.
A5: Automated integration tests covering schema-preservation for chat-to-tool flows, KV-cache continuity in trimmed-run mode, and metric collection for staged fallback are added to CI.
design_notes:
We propose a three-stage degradation approach: (1) Prefetch short-circuit: if Dedicated indicates imminent throttle but can still accept small requests, we prefetch model KV prefixes and serve low-latency prefix-heavy requests on Dedicated with strict token-budgeting. (2) Trimmed-run: for longer sequences we switch to a token-trimmed execution path that keeps response shape intact (function/tool-call markers) but synthesizes smaller bodies and uses quantized hosted variants only if allowed. (3) Hosted-backstop: final fallback routes to hosted endpoints with explicit headers indicating degraded mode. A response sanitization middleware will: normalize tool-call framing, inject a standardized metadata block for degraded responses (degradation_level, primary_model, fallback_model, reason_code), and scrub variant identifiers not permitted by tenant policy.

Trade-offs: extra latency from sanitization is minimal compared to host switch; complexity added in the routing layer and model policy table. We avoid model quality regressions by preferring truncated-but-structured responses over full freeform responses from mismatched hosted variants.

Security/privacy: variant-sanitization must remove internal-only variant names and ensure no internal diagnostics leak to customers. KMS-bound headers are not included in degraded payloads.
implementation_steps: 1) Add 'degradation_level' field to internal routing context and propagate through orchestrator.
2) Implement sanitization middleware in runtime handler (golang + proto) to normalize function-call markers and attach degradation metadata.
3) Extend model policy table service to include tenant-level allowed-variant lists and enforcement hooks in router.
4) Create 'trimmed-run' execution path that applies token budgets and KV-cache fallback semantics (reuse existing trimmed kernel when available).
5) Wire routing rules in capacity-adjudicator: threshold heuristics and hysteresis to trigger staged fallback instead of instant cutover.
6) Add feature flags for staged-degradation and sanitization to enable dark-launch.
7) Rollout: dark-launch -> internal-canary -> 5 customers opt-in -> gradual percentage rollout with telemetry gating.
testing_plan: Unit tests for sanitization middleware (schema preservation, metadata injection, variant-name scrub).
Integration tests simulating Dedicated capacity pressure and asserting staged fallback transitions and KV cache reuse.
Load tests comparing latency and token-cost for steady-state vs degraded paths (P50/P95/P99).
Chaos test: force misconfigured model policy and assert router blocks non-allowed hosted variants and returns gated diagnostic error.
Customer QA: run the feature with 3 internal teams using representative prompts that exercise tool-call flows; verify no functional regressions.
metrics_and_alerts: routing.degradation.transitions_total - counter of transitions per tenant and region
routing.degradation.latency.P95 - compare against baseline; alert if P95 degrades > 2x baseline for >5min
routing.sanitization.failures - count of sanitization errors (schema mismatch, scrub failure)
model_policy.enforcement.denied_requests - alert on spikes indicating policy misconfigurations
business.customer_impact_incidents - track via manual tagging when customers report regressions
dependencies: runtime: trimmed-kernel and KV-cache fallback APIs (infra change request)
notes_and_open_questions: Q1: Should the sanitization middleware have a 'lenient' mode that attempts to rewrite malformed structured responses, or should it fail fast and return an explicit degradation wrapper?
Q2: Are there tenant tiers that should never be routed to hosted (even temporarily)? How do we represent that in policy?
Q3: How do we communicate degraded mode to SDK consumers in a backwards-compatible way? Proposed header: X-Redwood-Degraded: level=v2;reason=dedicated_capacity
Decision: We'll default to fail-safe explicit wrapper (no silent rewrites) for first release to reduce correctness risk; iterate on lenient rewrite later.
